Fernando Corrêa da Costa, 2367, Bairro Boa Esperança, CEP 78060-900, Cuiabá, MT, Brazil. - name: Elvio Sergio Figueredo Medeiros orcid: 0000-0002-7472-8147 corresponding: true email: elviomedeiros@servidor.uepb.edu.br roles: [] affiliations: - Grupo de Ecologia de Rios do Semiárido, Laboratório de Ecologia, Departamento de Ciências Biológicas, Universidade Estadual da Paraíba – UEPB, Campus V, Rua Horácio Trajano de Oliveira, S/N, Cristo, CEP 58071-470, João Pessoa, PB, Brazil. keywords: - Floresta Atlântica - Zooplâncton - Riachos tropicais - Partição da diversidade - Sazonalidade climática date: "2026-10-04" abstract: "Abstract" lang: "en-US" editor: source toc: true number-sections: true bibliography: refs/references.bib csl: refs/ecology.csl highlight-style: pygments format: html: code-fold: true code-overflow: scroll embed-resources: true execute: echo: true pdf: lof: true lot: true toc: true code-line-numbers: true colorlinks: true execute: echo: true docx: lof: true lot: false #se T não aparece no docx toc: true reference-doc: refs/custom-rmarkdown-word.docx execute: echo: false #add echo: to code chunk options (#|) to overide specific chunk execute: result: hold warning: false message: false always_allow_html: yes editor_options: chunk_output_type: console --- # Introduction Essas abordagens são baseadas nos conceitos de turnover and nestedness. Species turnover and nestedness are two distinct components used to break down and understand beta diversity—which measures how much species composition changes between different communities or sites [@baselga2010], where, turnover is the replacement of some species by different species from one site to another, while nestedness is the loss or gain of species where poorer sites contain a strict subset of the species found at richer sites. CITAR: [@ligeiro2010; @crist2003; @ávila2011; @shell2018; @baselga2012; @baselga2010; @gering2003; @veech2003] ## Objectives This study describes the richness and density of zooplankton, comparatively between two small head water streams subject to different levels of environmental pressures. One originates withing a protected area - Biological Reserve, or REBIO, according to @brasil2000 - and its course extends beyond its administrative boundaries [@mma2003], and a second one that flows entirely outside of the protected area. Within this framework, we use hierarchical additive partitioning to evaluate the relative contribution of different spatial and temporal scales to the diversity of zooplankton assemblages. Given the importance of the Atlantic Forest to the biodiversity [@pereira2026] and its fragmented stated north of the São Francisco river basin [@silva2003], we aim with this study, (1) to infer environmental degradation from species turnover [@baselga2010] and (2) to associate beta-diversity to the ecological health of sites inside and surrounding a protected area of Atlantic Forest. Given the expected different levels of environmental pressures in the area [@gouveia2017], we hypothesize that the diversity is not be homogeneously distributed among the different spatial scales but concentrated at the finer levels and seasonal variation will be limited to species composition, but no spacial variation is expected between dry and wet seasons. Some environmental features (reach morphology, habitat structure, and water quality) are also described to explore possible explaining factors for the observed patterns. # Material and methods ## Study area and sampling design This study was conducted in the Guaribas Biological Reserve (REBIO Guaribas), a protected area of Atlantic Forest in northeastern Brazil. This protected area is located in a transitional zone between the Caatinga and Atlantic Forest ecoregions. The land use of the study area is based on the occupation of traditional human populations and an increasing use of land for large scale monocultures, mostly sugar cane [@heinrichs2017]. Other than these, small scale agricultural activities, fishing, and the modification of the natural vegetation for livestock are important anthropogenic pressures that affect the buffer zone of the REBIO [@arruda2013; @mma2026]. Other common uses of the soil in the area are, coconut plantations, orchards and subsistence agriculture. These land uses represent important sources of pollution, either through agrochemicals runoff or direct and indirect domestic effluents (such as septic tanks). These nonpoint source pollutants contaminate underground water and create a spatial gradient of environmental disturbance [@mehla2026]. Therefore, the mainly rural nature of the land use associated with the management of vegetation, will cause direct impact to aquatic systems, by the siltation of streams and contamination of groundwater. The hydrographic network of the study region is composed predominantly of small catchments containing first- and second-order streams [@strahler1957 classification] (@fig-mapa). These watercourses are tributaries of the Camaratuba River and are sustained by numerous springs distributed throughout the region. The two main stream systems in the study area are the Barro Branco and Caiana catchemnts. The Barro Branco stream is approximately 8.8 km long and originates within the protected area. Its upper section remains within the boundaries of the REBIO, whereas its middle and lower sections extend into the surrounding landscape. Despite this transition, riparian vegetation is preserved along most of the stream. The Caiana stream is approximately 9.8 km long and also originates within the REBIO, although most of its course lies outside the protection area. The climate in the region is classified as As' [@peel2007], characterized by a mean annual temperature of approximately 25 °C, with maximum temperatures occurring mainly between February and March, during the dry period, as well as by low annual thermal amplitude. Annual precipitation ranges from 1,400 to 1,800 mm, concentrated between March and July, whereas the lowest rainfall levels occur between September and December. In the study area, rainfall is concentrated between March and July, beginning in autumn and extending into winter. This pattern is attributed to the influence of cold air masses from the South Atlantic ocean that affect the region. The hydrographic network is composed of small headwater streams fed by rain [@gouveia2017]. A total of 15 sampling sites distributed longitudinally across the two Atlantic Forest streams were selected to capture spatial variation in environmental conditions and habitat characteristics. The Barro Branco stream included sampling sites located within a protected area (REBIO Guaribas) and sites located outside its boundaries, whereas all sampling sites in the Caiana stream were located outside the protected area. This sampling design allowed the assessment of zooplankton diversity across nested spatial scales and contrasting conditions of environmental protection and human influence (@fig-mapa). Sampling included temporal (dry and wet seasons) and spatial scales. The spatial scales of zooplankton diversity were represented by the total gamma (γ) diversity, encompassing both study streams. At each stream, several sites were selected according to their position in the main channel of the catchment basin and, at each site, three habitas were sampled to represent different habitat types (pool, riffle, near underwater structures) [@frissell1986]. We also considered a further spatial scale being the upper reaches (portion of the Barro Branco stream within the conservation unit and the Caiana stream before its confluence with the Pipina stream) and the lower reaches (portion of the Barro Branco stream outside the conservation unit and the Caiana stream after its confluence with the Pipina stream) (@fig-mapa). Sampling was conducted during the dry (January-February) and wet (June-July) seasons of 2024. ## Environmental data collection Environmental conditions were characterized using four groups of variables, following procedures adapted by @medeiros2008 from the protocols proposed by @pusey2004 and @mugodo2006: physicochemical water quality, stream site morphology, substrate composition, and marginal habitat structure. Water quality was characterized using physical and chemical measurements obtained with portable instruments, including water temperature (°C) and dissolved oxygen concentration (mg/L). Turbidity was subsequently measured in the laboratory with a turbidimeter using water samples collected at each sampling site. Current velocity (m/s) was estimated using the float method, as described by @maitland1990. Morphological characteristics were assessed from three randomly selected transects at each site, where stream width (cm) and water depth (cm) were measured. Bank slope was classified into four categories according to its inclination: 1, ≤ 20°; 2, \> 20–30°; 3, \> 30–50°; and 4, \> 50°. Broader-scale landscape characteristics, including elevation and stream length, were obtained from handheld GPS records and satellite imagery. Substrate composition and the physical structure of marginal habitats were evaluated from 9 to 12 quadrats (1 m²) distributed along the terrestrial-aquatic interface at each sampling site. Within each quadrat, the proportional cover of different substrate categories was visually estimated, including mud, sand, cobbles, fine and coarse gravel and rocks. The same quadrats were used to characterize littoral and submerged habitat features. Recorded habitat components included macrophytes, marginal grasses, leaf litter, attached and filamentous algae, overhanging and submerged vegetation, small and large woody debris, and root masses [@medeiros2008]. For subsequent analyses and presentation, environmental measurements were summarized as mean values for each sampling site. Three 250 mL replicate samples of water from each site were taken and refrigerated for concentration analysis (μg L⁻¹) of ammonia, nitrite, nitrate, orthophosphate (soluble reactive phosphorus) and total phosphorus. Nutrient concentrations were obtained based on Standard Methods for the Examination of Water [-@apha1998] and @mackereth1978. ## Zooplankton sampling Zooplankton was sampled at habitats within each sampling site, hereafter referred to as habitat samples. Collections were performed in the main channel of the streams at the surface water. At each sampling habitat, a plankton net (30 cm mouth diameter, 70 cm length, and 60 μm mesh size) was used to filter 50 L of water. The net was rinsed between successive samples to prevent clogging and carryover of organisms. Each sample was concentrated to a final volume of 80 mL for laboratory analyses. Following collection, zooplankton samples were anesthetized with commercial sparkling water and subsequently preserved in 4% formalin [@epa2020]. Sucrose was added to the preserved sample to prevent female cladocerans from losing eggs and to minimize carapace distortion [@haney1973]. In the laboratory, samples had their zooplankton identified and counted using a Sedgewick–Rafter counting chamber. The analyses focused on representatives of Rotifera, Cladocera, and Copepoda. Taxonomic identification was based on specialized literature and confirmed by specialists. To evaluate whether the sampling effort adequately represented the zooplankton assemblage, species accumulation curves were calculated [@lucena2015; @melo2014]. ## Statistical analyses Environmental variables were screened for multicollinearity and to identify redundant descriptors. Variables representing similar environmental information were also combined when appropriate, thereby reducing redundancy in the dataset [@legendre1998]. ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ::: These data were then analyzed using Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to summarize multivariate patterns of environmental variation among sampling sites. Prior to PCA, site morphology and water-quality variables were square-root transformed [@sokal1995]. Variables describing sediment composition and marginal habitat structure, expressed as percentages, were relativized by their column totals and subsequently subjected to the arcsine square-root transformation [@mccune2002]. PCA was conducted in R using the `FactoMineR` package [@lê2008], with all variables centered and standardized to unit variance before analysis. The water quality parameters temperature and dissolved oxygen, and all nutrients were used to characterize differences between streams but were not used in the PCA because they were not measured for both seasons. A Permutational Multivariate Analysis of Variance (PERMANOVA, 999 permutations) was performed to test whether the overall set of environmental variables measured differed across the seasons and streams [@freiry2020; @anderson2013]. To compare the diversity of zooplanktonic taxa between streams, the Chao1 estimated richness (±SE) and the curves of rarefied and extrapolated richness were generated (95% upper and lower confidence intervals) using individual-based rarefaction curves [@gotelli2001; @freiry2020]. Differences in assemblage composition across the spatial hierarchy and seasons were explored using the Unweighted Pair Group Method with Averages (UPGMA) [@belbin1993; @diniz-reis2022], based on Bray-Curtis dissimilarities calculated from the zooplankton density matrix [@ávila2011]. Prior to the analyses, density data were relativized and square-root transformed to reduce the influence of highly abundant taxa and improve the distributional properties of the dataset [@rocha2012]. To focus on spatial variation across sampling sites, habitat density data were pooled for this analysis. To assess how well the UPGMA dendrograms represented the original Bray-Curtis dissimilarities among sampling sites, the Cophenetic Correlation Coefficient (CC) was calculated [@sneath1973; @sokal1962; @saraçli2013], where a cophenetic matrix was constructed from each seasonal dendrogram using the *cophenetic* function in the `vegan` package in R. The cophenetic distance matrix was then correlated with the corresponding original Bray-Curtis dissimilarity matrix using Pearson's product-moment correlation coefficient [@farris1969; @silva2013; @sokal1962]. To evaluate the strength of the hierarchical clustering structure obtained from the UPGMA dendrograms, the Agglomerative Coefficient (AC) was calculated for each season using the *coef.hclust* function from the `cluster` package in R [@maechler2026; @kaufman1990]. The AC ranges from 0 to 1, where values closer to 1 indicate a strong, well-defined clustering structure and values near 0 reflect weak or indistinct grouping. Additive diversity partitioning was used to quantify the contribution of within- and between-unit diversity to total zooplankton diversity. In this framework, alpha diversity ($\alpha$) represents diversity occurring within sampling units, whereas beta diversity ($\beta$) represents the contribution of differences among units at successive levels of the spatial hierarchy [@lande1996; @crist2003]. The hierarchical structure included three spatial scales. The finest scales consisted of the habitat samples within each site (n = 3), and of each site (n = 6, for the Barro Branco stream, and n = 9, for the Caiana stream). The intermediate scales corresponded to the upper and lower stream sections (n = 2), whereas the broadest scale represented differences among the two streams. Accordingly, the total diversity ($\gamma$) was decomposed into within-habitat diversity ($\alpha_{1}$) and the successive beta components associated with differences among habitats ($\beta_{1}$), among sites withing upper and lower stream reaches ($\beta_{2}$), and among streams ($\beta_{3}$). The contribution of each component was expressed as a percentage of total diversity [@crist2003; @farias2020]. To investigate seasonal variation in the hierarchical structure of diversity, additive partitioning was performed separately for each season and for each stream [@farias2020; @melo2013]. The overall diversity was taken to be the sum of the relative contributions of each scale in the hierarchical sampling design. Analysis of significance of the contribution of each hierarchical level was performed through with individual-based randomizations (type I null model) [see @freiry2020; @melo2013]. The randomization process was repeated 999 times to obtain null distributions of the $\alpha$ and $\beta$ diversity at each hierarchical level, and used to test whether the observed values were higher or lower than expected by chance [@crist2003]. The probabilities obtained from randomization tests were interpreted as *P*-values, as a low *P*-value ($\text{Prop}_{exp} > \text{Prop}_{obs} < 0.05$) indicates an observed diversity significantly different than that expected under the null model. On the other hand, a high *P*-value ($\text{Prop}_{exp} > \text{Prop}_{obs} > 0.95$) indicates an observed diversity not different than that expected by chance [@crist2003; @freiry2020; @gering2003; @veech2002]. The results of the analysis were subject to a Monte Carlo permutation test (999 permutations) for validation. The additive partitioning of the diversity was carried out with the function *adipart* from package `vegan` [@oksanen]. All analyses were conducted in the statistical environment R [@rcoreteam2017]. # Results ## Environmental variables and nutrient concentration Water velocity ranged from 0 to 0.41 m/s, with the highest average recorded at site 14. Waters were, on average, well oxygenated (5.3 to 8.1 mg/L), and cool, with average temperatures betwen from 25.2 to 32.5 °C, the average being 27.7 °C. Conductivity ranged from 98.8 and 223.0 μS/cm, pH was mostly neutral to slightly acidic (from 5.1 to 6.9) and turbidity was low (4.9 to 79.2 NTU). Regarding the morphologacal variables, elevation ranged from 41.5 to 112.8 m a.s.l., while the stream margins slope reached 50° for some sites. Stream width and depth showed greater variations reflecting the range of habitats along the study streams, from small and narrow streams to wider and deeper manmade reservoirs in the stream channel. Stream site width varied from 1 m across to 19.5 m in larger reservoirs. Overall, depths ranged from approx. 10-20 cm to a maximum of 1.55 m, on average. Substrate composition across sites consisted mainly of mud (reaching 100% at sites 1 and 2, in the Barro Branco stream) and sand being more common at the Caiana Stream (reaching 98.3% cover at site 14) (@tbl-hab_gttable). Marginal and underwater habitat structures were diverse with most variables being common at the Barro Branco stream, namely aquatic macrophytes, fillamentous and attached algae and littoral grass. Submerged and overhanging vegetation, leaf litter, root masses and wood debris were present at all sites (see @tbl-hab_gttable). ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ::: Principal Component Analysis (PCA) was used to summarize environmental variation among sampling sites and to identify variables contributing to the differences between streams (@fig-hab_PCA_rio) and seasons (@fig-hab_PCA_periodo). The first two principal components explained 38.6% of the total variance, with the first axis accounting for 23.2%. In relation to the environmental variables of water quality, the Barro Branco stream was more associated with higher elevations, the predominance of muddy substrate and a narrower array of underwater structures, mostly algae, macrophytes, leaf litter and woody debris. The Caiana stream showed a wider range of variables affecting it's waters, being associated with higher pH, turbidity and depths, as well as a predominance of sandy substrates and, to a lesser degree, root masses. Water velocity was also important for this stream. PERMANOVA showed significant differences in the environmental variables between the two study streams ($\text{F}_{1,88} = 7.8, R^2 = 0.08, p = 0.001$). Dry and wet seasons did not show clear segregation in the PCA, even though PERMANOVA indicated significance of differences between seasons ($\text{F}_{1,88} = 3.8, R^2 = 0.04, p = 0.008$). ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ::: Among the averaged nutrient concentrations (@tbl-nutri_gttable), ammonia ranged from 49.2 to 243.7 µg L⁻¹. The Caiana stream tended to have greater values, but overall no clear trend can be observed when comparing both streams. Nitrite and nitrate, on the other hand, show clearly a greater concentrations at the Caiana stream, nitrate varying from 166.4 to 2003.0 µg L⁻¹, compared with the maximum of 18.8 µg L⁻¹ at the Barro Branco stream. Nitrite was too low to be detectable at the Barro Branco stream. The same pattern was observed for orthophosphate concentrations, being barely detectable at Barro Branco stream, and varying from 4.0 to 32.0 µg L⁻¹ at the Caiana stream. Total phosphorus, however, tended to have higher concentrations at Barro Branco stream, reaching 50.1 µg L⁻¹ at Site 3, but with highly variable values (from non detectable to 38.7 µg L⁻¹, as the second highest value). ::: {.cell} ::: ## Community structure A total of 56 taxa distributed among Rotifera (14 families), Cladocera (5 families) and Copepoda (2 families) were identified during the study period. Rotifera was the most species-rich group, represented by 39 species (plus Bdelloidea), followed by Cladocera (12 species) and Copepoda (4 species, in addition to the juvenile stages nauplii and copepodite). Across sampling periods, Lecanidae exhibited the highest richness among all recorded families of Rotifera with 15 species, followed by Lepadellidae, Synchaetidae (both with 4 species), Brachionidae and Mytilinidae (both with 3 species). Bdelloidea was the most abundant taxa (6194 individuals) followed by *Lecane curvicornis* with 626 individuals. Among the cladocerans, Chydoridae was the richest family with 5 species, followed by Macrothricidae (3 species). *Alonella dadayi* was the most abundant among the cladocerans with 1051 individuals. Juvenile stages (nauplii and copepodite) were also abundant with 2433 and 4061 individuals, respectively. Copepods were represented by he orders Cyclopoida and Calanoida, *Paracyclops* sp. *Mesocyclops* sp. being the most abundant (141 and 231 individuals, respectively). ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ::: Rarefaction analysis showed that the Caiana stream had a taxa richness slightly higher than that of the Barro Branco stream (@fig-rare1). Nevertheless, the Chao index estimated an extrapolated richness of 58 (±8.9) species for the Barro Branco stream, compared with 54.2 (± 4.3) species for the Caiana stream. ::: {.cell} ::: The NMDS ordination diagrams showed that the composition of zooplankton resting stages differed among most of the ponds from the forest (Fig. 4A) and grassland biomes (Fig. 4B). In addition, the PERMANOVA indicated a significant difference in the composition of zooplanktonic taxa between biomes (pseudo-F1, 53 = 1.85, R2 = 0.035; P = 0.03). The outputs of the db-RDAs showed that the water chemistry subset significantly influenced the dissimilarity in the resting stage composition (F = 1.25; R2 = 0.134; P = 0.02), while the subset of habitat structure did not (F = 0.88; R2  0.01; P = 0.88, Fig. 5). The UPGMA cluster analyses revealed low-to-moderate spatial clustering strength for the zooplankton communities across both periods, as indicated by the Agglomerative Coefficients ($AC_{dry} = 0.34$ and $AC_{wet} = 0.39$). While community composition exhibited continuous variation across sites, spatial structuring was slightly more pronounced during the wet season than during the dry season. ::: {.cell} ::: ## Diversity Partitioning ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ::: # Discussion Depth and width showed greater variations across sites as a result from the fact the streams are barred at some points from roads for local traffic and small dams for water storage. Stream width and depth showed greater variations reflecting the range of habitats along the study streams, from small and narrow streams to wider and deeper manmade reservoirs. # Conclusions {.unnumbered} # Acknowledgements {.unnumbered} We are greatly indebted to the staff of the REBIO Guaribas for field work assistance.
